title: Gameplay footage of our Tactical Dungeon Crawler + Sprite workflow
author: Cosmonan
selftext:
Been working for 2 months in this Roguelike Dungeon crawler. The idea was to make a modern Mystery Dungeon / Traditional Roguelike game. First I tried mashing modern action roguelike/lite with turn based game, which in my head seemed awesome. Then, I brought the game to a friend of mine, and while watching him play, I noticed that a lot of systems were only distracting him from the real fun: the combat. 

This video was recorded after I removed all those excess systems, such as Hunger and Throwable items (from mystery dungeon formula) and added more skill options and geometry. Now the focus of the game is map exploration and elemental combo-based tactical combat.

One of the best workflows I got working is creating new sprites for enemies while keeping consistency, using Pixel Lab:

1. Generate the main character in 8 positions from Pixel Lab web. Ask for a symmetrical character.

2. Connect to Pixel Lab MCP and API in Claude Code / Codex.

3. Use Generate Image from Style using the character as reference to create some enemies.

4. Select 3 or 4 from those that fit your game style, generate more if required.

5. Use Generate Image Pro setting the player character as style reference, and select the player SE position + the 3/4 choices of reference enemies as Reference Images.

6. After generating the sprites, use the generate animation from image in each one of those. Ask Claude to first see the enemy sprite to create an animation prompt adequate to the sprite.

8. Save the process as a .SKILL after validating it.

7. This way you can basically automate your enemy rooster creation. I would say you'll still need to regenerate 20% of the animations, and touch up se frames in Aseprite, but nothing too bad.

replies.author: Cosmonan
replies.body: Thank you! I'm really taking my time to polish the visuals.

comments.author: stolenyourgf
comments.body: Your PixelLab style-reference pipeline is solid. The Aseprite pass is where most of the "almost ready" frames fail: lock the palette, snap to a single pixel grid, then check silhouette and foot anchors across the sheet so the character doesn't swim. I keep a layered .aseprite plus a timelapse of that pass — it also doubles as process proof if you need it for a Steam AI disclosure or a devlog.

comments.author: Cosmonan
comments.body: Not bad, really! It got the sword hand right fore every position. I wasn't able to have Pixel Lab get this right, so I had to go with bare handed characters 🤣. Gonna give Sprite Fusion a chance I guess.
